equation_request.abstract: A major problem facing the development of quantum computers or large scale quantum simulators is that general methods for characterizing and controlling are intractable. We provide a new approach to this problem that uses small quantum simulators to efficiently characterize and learn control models for larger devices. Our protocol achieves this by using Bayesian inference in concert with Lieb-Robinson bounds and interactive quantum learning methods to achieve compressed simulations for characterization. We also show that the Lieb–Robinson velocity is epistemic for our protocol, meaning that information propagates at a rate that depends on the uncertainty in the system Hamiltonian. We illustrate the efficiency of our bootstrapping protocol by showing numerically that an 8-qubit Ising model simulator can be used to calibrate and control a 50 qubit Ising simulator while using only about 750 kilobits of experimental data. Finally, we provide upper bounds for the Fisher information that show that the number of experiments needed to characterize a system rapidly diverges as the duration of the experiments used in the characterization shrinks, which motivates the use of methods such as ours that do not require short evolution times.

specification.problem: Characterize (learn the Hamiltonian parameters of) a large quantum device whose dynamics cannot be classically simulated, using a smaller trusted quantum simulator to evaluate Bayesian likelihoods for local measurements. The abstract describes a bootstrapping protocol combining Bayesian inference, Lieb-Robinson bounds (to truncate the large system to a small local patch), and interactive quantum learning; it reports numerics for an 8-qubit Ising simulator calibrating a 50-qubit Ising simulator and gives Fisher-information upper bounds showing short-time experiments are inefficient.
specification.reconstruction_scope: ONE smallest useful instance (chosen as an assumption): an unknown 1D transverse-field Ising chain on N=4 qubits with open boundaries; a trusted n=2 qubit simulator emulates the local patch {1,2} via a truncated Hamiltonian H_S(x). The unknown parameters are x=(J_1,h_1) (edge coupling and edge field); all other couplings/fields are assumed known. Each experiment prepares |00> on the patch, evolves under H_S(x) for time t, and measures Z on qubit 1; the outcome probability is used as the likelihood in a Bayes update (sequential Monte Carlo / particle filter). A Lieb-Robinson bound provides the truncation error controlling how large t may be for a patch of linear size l. Outside scope: the full 8-qubit-to-50-qubit numerical result and its 750 kbit data budget, the precise 'epistemic Lieb-Robinson velocity' statement, the paper's specific Fisher-information bounds, the interactive (inverse-evolution/swap) variant, control-model learning, and adaptive experiment design heuristics.

equations.label: Transverse-field Ising Hamiltonian of the large device
equations.latex: H(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1} J_i\, Z_i Z_{i+1}+\sum_{i=1}^{N} h_i\, X_i,\qquad N=4
equations.description: Open-chain Ising model with ZZ couplings and transverse fields; qubit i is the i-th tensor factor (qubit 1 leftmost).
equations.justification: The abstract says only 'Ising model simulator'; the transverse-field 1D open-chain form and N=4 are chosen as the smallest useful instance.

equations.label: Truncated (compressed) patch Hamiltonian on the small simulator
equations.description: Restriction of H(x) to the patch S by dropping all terms not fully supported on S; this is what the trusted n-qubit simulator implements.
equations.abstract_quote: uses small quantum simulators to efficiently characterize and learn control models for larger devices
equations.justification: Using a small simulator for a larger device requires simulating a reduced model; truncation to a local patch is the natural compression consistent with the abstract's use of Lieb-Robinson bounds. The specific truncation rule is an assumption.
assumptions: terms are dropped by simple support restriction (no boundary corrections)
only J_1 and h_1 are unknown; h_2 is known

equations.label: Likelihood of a local measurement from the compressed simulation
equations.latex: P(d\mid x,t)\approx \mathrm{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_d\, e^{-iH_S(x)t}\,|00\rangle\langle 00|\, e^{iH_S(x)t}\right],\qquad \Pi_d=|d\rangle\langle d|_1\otimes I_2
equations.description: The probability of observing outcome d on qubit 1 after time t under the true device H(x) is approximated by the same quantity computed on the truncated patch; the approximation error is bounded by eq_4.
equations.justification: Born rule for a projective Z measurement after unitary evolution; the approximation sign reflects truncation rather than exact equality.
assumptions: initial state |00> on the patch (device initialised to |0>^{\otimes N})

equations.label: Lieb-Robinson truncation error bound
equations.latex: \left|\mathrm{Tr}[\Pi_d\, e^{-iH t}\rho e^{iH t}]-\mathrm{Tr}[\Pi_d\, e^{-iH_S t}\rho e^{iH_S t}]\right|\le C\, e^{(v t-\ell)/\xi},\qquad \ell=\mathrm{dist}(\{1\},\partial S)
equations.description: Standard Lieb-Robinson-type statement: the influence of Hamiltonian terms outside the patch on an observable localized at site 1 is exponentially small until the light cone v t reaches the patch boundary at distance l. Controls the admissible t for a given patch size.
equations.justification: Recalled form of Lieb-Robinson locality bounds for local Hamiltonians with bounded interaction strength; the abstract invokes Lieb-Robinson bounds but does not state this inequality or its constants.
assumptions: bounded interaction strengths |J_i|,|h_i|\le J_{max} so that v,\xi,C exist

equations.label: Bayesian update (sequential, particle approximation)
equations.latex: P(x\mid d_k,t_k,D_{k-1})=\frac{P(d_k\mid x,t_k)\,P(x\mid D_{k-1})}{\int P(d_k\mid x',t_k)\,P(x'\mid D_{k-1})\,dx'},\qquad P(x\mid D_{k-1})\approx\sum_{j=1}^{N_p} w_j\,\delta(x-x_j)
equations.description: After each experiment the posterior over (J_1,h_1) is updated with the likelihood from eq_3; a particle filter with N_p weighted particles represents the distribution, with the estimate taken as the posterior mean.
equations.abstract_quote: using Bayesian inference in concert with Lieb-Robinson bounds
equations.justification: Bayes' rule follows directly from the stated use of Bayesian inference; the sequential Monte Carlo particle representation is a standard implementation choice, not stated in the abstract.
assumptions: uniform prior on a bounded box, e.g. J_1,h_1\in[0,1]

equations.label: Short-time Fisher information scaling (background form)
equations.description: Generic quantum Fisher information bound for a parameter entering a Hamiltonian evolution of duration t, implying (via Cramer-Rao) that the number of experiments to reach precision epsilon diverges as t -> 0. The paper's specific bounds are not available and may differ in form.
equations.justification: The abstract claims Fisher-information upper bounds showing divergence of experiment count as duration shrinks; this recalled background bound exhibits that qualitative behaviour but is not the paper's stated result.
assumptions: single-parameter Cramer-Rao scaling used for the experiment count

registers.name: sim
registers.role: Trusted small-simulator register implementing the truncated patch Hamiltonian H_S(x); qubit 1 is the measured edge site, qubit 2 its neighbour (qubit 1 = leftmost tensor factor).

registers.name: device
registers.role: Large untrusted Ising device whose edge-site Z statistics are collected experimentally (not simulated in the scoped construction; it is the data source).

specification.initial_state: |00\rangle on the sim register (and |0\rangle^{\otimes 4} on the device register at the start of each experiment).

steps.description: Fix the model class: the device is assumed to be the N=4 open transverse-field Ising chain of eq_1 with unknown x=(J_1,h_1) and known h_2,h_3,h_4,J_2,J_3; choose a uniform prior on a bounded box and initialise N_p particles.

Choose an experiment time t such that the Lieb-Robinson light cone does not exit the patch, i.e. v t < l (with slack so that the error in eq_4 is below the target tolerance); this is the compression condition that allows the n=2 simulator to stand in for the N=4 device.
Run the experiment on the device: prepare |0>^{\otimes 4}, evolve for time t under the true H(x), measure Z on qubit 1, record outcome d.
For each particle x_j, run the trusted simulator: prepare |00>, evolve under H_S(x_j) for time t (eq_2), measure Z on qubit 1 repeatedly to estimate P(d | x_j, t) per eq_3.

Update the particle weights with Bayes' rule (eq_5), resample if the effective sample size is low, and report the posterior mean as the current estimate of (J_1,h_1). Repeat steps 2-5; prefer longer t (within the eq_4 constraint) because short-t experiments carry little Fisher information (eq_6).

specification.measurement: Single-qubit computational-basis (Z) measurement on qubit 1 of the sim register (and on qubit 1 of the device), outcome d in {0,1}; repeated shots estimate P(d | x_j, t).
specification.classical_postprocessing: Particle-filter Bayesian update of weights w_j <- w_j P(d|x_j,t) followed by normalisation and resampling; estimate x-hat = sum_j w_j x_j and posterior covariance as the uncertainty. Stopping when the posterior variance falls below a chosen threshold.
assumptions: No experiment_scope was provided; the smallest useful construction (N=4 device, n=2 patch, two unknown edge parameters) is a chosen instance, not from the abstract.
Transverse-field Ising form with open boundaries and bounded couplings.
Truncation is by simple support restriction to the patch; no boundary-correction terms.
Non-interactive (likelihood-only) quantum Hamiltonian learning is used in scope; the abstract's 'interactive quantum learning methods' are not reconstructed.
Ideal preparation, evolution and measurement on both simulator and device.
Likelihoods on the simulator are estimated from finite shots; sampling error is ignored in the equations.
missing_information: The paper's actual bootstrapping protocol: how the 8-qubit simulator is iteratively used to calibrate progressively larger patches of the 50-qubit device, and how learned parameters are transferred.
Precise statement and formula of the 'epistemic Lieb-Robinson velocity' (dependence of the effective velocity on Hamiltonian uncertainty).
The paper's explicit Fisher-information upper bounds and the regime in which experiment count diverges.
Interactive learning details (e.g., inverse evolution on the simulator, swap/overlap measurements) and how they are combined with truncation.
Experiment-design heuristic for choosing t and measured sites, particle numbers, resampling rules, and how the ~750 kilobit data budget was counted.
Control-model learning component (how calibrated Hamiltonian parameters are turned into control of the 50-qubit simulator).
